newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia PM defends cabinet reshuffle to parliament.
newsitem.headline: Russia PM defends cabinet reshuffle to parliament.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, facing a hostile parliament, defended Russia's latest cabinet changes on Friday, saying they were aimed at restoring order in the economy and would help embattled national industries.

"The changes in the government have been prompted by the needs of the current stage of economic reforms," Chernomyrdin told the State Duma lower house, explaining last Monday's wholesale cabinet reshuffle.
The reshuffle was ordered by President Boris Yeltsin, who blasted the cabinet for failing to end delays in wages and pensions which led to worsening social tensions in the country.

"One of the main tasks now is to restore order in the financial sphere and in the budget, which means to restore order in paying wages, pensions and normalising the system of payments," Chernomyrdin told the Duma.

The Duma was angered by Yeltsin's decision to give top cabinet posts to reformers, including his chief of staff Anatoly Chubais -- a hated figure among Russian conservatives and communists -- whom he made first deputy prime minister.

The Duma demanded explanations from Chernomyrdin on the government changes. But the communist-dominated chamber has stopped short of demanding the government's resignation or even urging the Kremlin to back down on the reshuffle.

Conservative deputies were however alarmed by promises by new cabinet members to give a new push to radical market reform and to scrap the remnants of paternalistic welfare, one of the last vestiges of the Communist past.

"It will be difficult, it will be painful but we cannot let fortunes leak into sewage," Chernomyrdin said, defending inevitable increases in housing and municipal service charges planned by his government.
Chernomyrdin said though that the planned welfare reform would take place in stages and would include a safety net for the poor.

Chernomyrdin told the Duma in an hour-long address that the reshuffle would end by early next week and would not involve the so-called "power ministers" -- Defence, Interior and the head of the Federal Security Service, part of the former KGB.
"There will be no personnel changes in any power structures now," he told the Duma.
Parliamentary conservatives were alarmed by Yeltsin's decision to scrap some ministries, including the Industry Ministry, which they argued would lead to a collapse of Russian industrial capability.
Chernomyrdin said that enterprises, most of which have been privatised, no longer needed many of the Soviet-style ministries.
